text:
alex: FYI, ran into a cluster issue during the evening test - lots of ml-pod pending because node launches were slow, suspect ENI/trunking limits + cold GPU boot.
maria: oof. which region + instance types?
alex: us-west-2, trying to scale g5.2x -> some launches took >2.5m, kubelet didn't start before readiness probe timed out.
jin: we've seen NIC attach delays when trunk ENI quota gets hit on the instance family. Also AWS sometimes throttles ENA shakeouts on cold starts.
alex: logs show kubelet stuck waiting for CNI: "error configuring network: timeout waiting for device eth0". AWS attach logs show ENI attach retries.
infra-bot: docker image pull times: median 14s, 95th 38s for our ml-serving image (from eu-west repo mirror).
sam: can you paste the node bootstrap log snippet?
alex: sure:
```
Mar 15 02:12:11 kubelet[1]: I0315 02:12:11.223] network-plugin: set up network for pod default/model-serve-abc
Mar 15 02:13:45 kubelet[1]: E0315 02:13:45.893] failed to add pod network: timed out waiting for device
Mar 15 02:13:45 kubelet[1]: E0315 02:13:45.893] pod readiness probe failed
```
maria: that matches ENI attach latency. When we hit burst of scale-ups with trunking, some instance types only allow 1 or 2 branch ENIs which increases attach time.
leah: do we have Karpenter metrics around provisioning latency vs instance type? useful to correlate.
jin: yes, Karpenter exposes "provisioner_request_duration_seconds" and we have a grafana dashboard. I looked: g5.* has a 97th ~160s in those spike windows.
sam: two mitigation ideas: 1) pre-warm a small warm pool of nodes (low-util g5 nodes) so GPU-less cold starts are avoided, 2) fall back to smaller instance family (g4dn) when ENI attach queue is backed up.
alex: we tested warm pool in staging — pre-warmed nodes cut cold-start path time from ~150s -> ~25s.
maria: tradeoff is cost for idle GPU hours. Could use tiny number of warm nodes with eviction after X minutes when steady state; or use burst spot for warm nodes?
jin: also worth considering alternative CNI settings: enable secondary IP allocation pre-provisioned or switch to aws-vpc-cni with trunking tuned. But that needs careful change window.
leah: for Karpenter migration, how do we express these policies? can we signal preferred instance families and an emergency fallback policy?
sam: Karpenter provisioner can take topologyConstraints + requirements + consolidate: false/true. We can add a fallback provisioner with lower priority that allows g4dn and has a <maxPrice> for spot.
alex: here's a candidate provisioner YAML we sketched:
```
apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1alpha5
kind: Provisioner
metadata:
  name: gpu-provisioner-main
spec:
  requirements:
    - key: "karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-family"
      operator: In
      values: ["g5","p4d"]
  limits:
    resources:
      cpu: 5000
  consolidated: true
  ttlSecondsAfterEmpty: 300
```
leah: and a fallback:
```
metadata:
  name: gpu-fallback
spec:
  requirements:
    - key: "karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-family"
      operator: In
      values: ["g4dn","g4"]
  ttlSecondsAfterEmpty: 120
  weight: 0.2
```
jin: note: Karpenter doesn't have "weight" like ASG. We can use provisionerSelector / nodeSelector in pods or use priorityClass + pod k-scheduler constraints. Another pattern: run a small controller that mutates pods to prefer fallback when main hasn't provisioned in Xs.
maria: is that more complexity than we want? other simpler approach: increase Node startup parallelism and bump ENI quota in AWS account (request ENI trunking quota increase) and add subnet IP pools.
sam: quota increase is good long-term; but for migration/early rollout we should implement warm pool + fallback families.
alex: cost estimate: warm pool of 3 g5.2x for 24/7 is ~ $1.1k/mo. If we auto-evict after 10m idle, actual cost likely <20% of that in steady traffic.
leah: can we run a canary for 1 week with warm pool + fallback in us-west-2 only and measure SLO improvement? plan: enable warm pool in Karpenter via a static deployment that keeps 2 nodes labelled warm=true.
jin: or use instances with instance protection + taints: taint warm nodes so only pre-warm daemon & a small test pod keep them alive.
maria: let's log action items:
 - [ ] alex to create test script to simulate scale spikes and collect provisioner metrics (due EOD)
 - [ ] jin to tweak grafana to show ENI attach latency and correlate with node launch
 - [ ] sam to draft fallback provisioner + pod-scheduling pattern
 - [ ] leah to open AWS support ticket for ENI/trunk quota increase and request Nitro attach debugging
 - [ ] maria to cost-model warm pool and propose eviction policy
alex: added. I'll post results tomorrow. Thanks all :thumbsup:
infra-bot: deploy-bot: scheduled job "scale-spike-test" started at 2026-03-15T02:30:00Z"
sam: quick note - don't forget to include network interface limits per AZ when modelling ip exhaustion. We saw a case where subnet-level IP exhaustion caused similar symptoms.
maria: good call. Also check EFA/ENI types if we ever need RDMA for some perf tests.
alex: closing for now, will re-open thread with the test run logs. :rocket:"
